text:
The credit system is the main reason I am hesitant to use Bark. I was shown a package of 170 credits for $319.60 excluding tax, which breaks down to $1.88 per credit and is described as enough for about 10 leads. But if a lead costs around 20+ credits to respond to, that means each lead can cost about $37.60 or more before tax — just to contact the customer.

That is a lot for a small business, especially when there is no guarantee the customer will reply, be serious, or hire. The “Get Hired Guarantee” sounds good, but if it only returns credits instead of refunding the money, then professionals are still locked into spending more time and credits on the same platform.

I think Bark needs to be more transparent about the actual cost per lead and what professionals are really paying for. The upfront cost feels high, and the risk is mostly placed on the professional.

text:
I had an extremely disappointing experience with Yell’s website service, and I regret choosing them.

Before signing the contract, I was told the website setup would take about a week before development started. Instead, the entire process dragged on for over a month and became incredibly stressful. I provided every page and all of the content they needed, but the website they produced looked very basic and unprofessional. It honestly felt like it had been built by someone with very little web design experience.

Rather than working with experienced web designers and developers, I found myself teaching their team how to build my own website. I spent four consecutive days explaining how the website should be designed, and even then it was still incomplete.

The booking form was one of the most important parts of my business. I even gave them a working example of how I wanted it built, but they failed to implement it correctly. I also tested the booking system they created, and it leaves customers stuck halfway through the process without taking them anywhere. In my opinion, this is a serious issue that could easily cost businesses potential customers. It seemed they either lacked the technical knowledge or the professional experience needed to build the functionality correctly.

Even their own website checking tools identified numerous issues that required improvement, yet these problems remained unresolved.

During the sales process, I was left with the impression that I was hiring a professional British company that would take care of everything for me. Unfortunately, the reality was very different. Once the contract was signed, I had to chase them constantly for updates and corrections. I called them three times within the first month asking to cancel the contract because I had already lost confidence in their ability to deliver, but my requests were refused.

At the moment, my app shows 21 leads. However, 15 of those were simply test submissions made by Yell themselves while testing my website. Of the remaining six, none resulted in a confirmed booking, and two weren’t even related to my services. From my perspective, this has been a complete loss of time and money.

Another major issue is the tracking phone number they provide. I cannot directly call customers back using that number, so I’m forced to contact them from my personal mobile instead. Many customers don’t answer unknown mobile numbers, which I believe has caused me to lose potential jobs and genuine leads.

I paid around £800 for a website that I don’t believe will help my business. I even accepted that financial loss and asked them to cancel my contract, but because it is a business-to-business agreement, I was told I would still have to continue paying regardless of whether the leads generated turned into actual work.

In my opinion, Yell needs to invest in experienced web developers, professional web designers, and better software if they want to compete in today’s market and deliver the quality of service customers are promised.

This entire experience has caused me an enormous amount of stress and has had a serious impact on my mental wellbeing. What was promised during the sales process was not what I experienced as a customer.

Based on my personal experience, I cannot recommend Yell’s website design service. I strongly advise anyone considering their website package to fully understand what they are agreeing to before signing a contract.

text:
My three-month experience with Yell Business has been incredibly disappointing. Despite promising increased traffic through Google ads and their platform, the reality fell short. As the owner of Speed Booking UK, which has flourished via Instagram and Facebook ads, I expected better results. Yell's website design was subpar even after multiple revisions, and the traffic I received was mostly spam calls and texts. Attempting to cancel my £360/month subscription proved futile, as I'm locked into a 12-month contract and faced threats of debt collectors. I urge potential Yell Business customers to explore alternatives like Google, Instagram, or Facebook ads. 

My client manager at Yell has been exceptionally supportive, and everyone I've interacted with has been understanding and helpful given my current circumstances. I have no complaints about any individual on the team. However, my main concern lies with the overall business practices. Entering into a 12-month contract without guaranteeing the expected results for the majority of customers feels unethical.

I'm still seeking to cancel my subscription, but doubt Yell's willingness to prioritize customer satisfaction over profit.

*Updated Review as of 15/09/2025*
Quick update – someone from the Yell team got in touch regarding my issue with the monthly subscription, and they were actually able to switch my package over to Google Ads instead of just promoting on Yell. Once they did that, I started seeing more clicks and better interaction with my business.

To be honest, I think Yell’s business model is focused way too much on pushing you to advertise on their own platform, even though barely anyone actually uses Yell to search for services anymore — most people just Google it. So the fact they prioritise their own listings over running proper Google Ads for you is a bit frustrating.

That said, the person I spoke to was helpful, and after switching to the Google Ads option, I did get better results. I ended up staying on for another 3–4 months before cancelling, which I did straight away once the term ended.

If you’re considering Yell, I’d definitely recommend pushing for the Google Ads package, not just their own platform listings. The listings are technically free, but honestly, the leads you get are low quality and not worth much. Get them to advertise your business on Google — that’s the only way you’ll see real value.

I’ve changed my review from 1 star to 3 stars because they eventually sorted the issue, but I still feel the service overall wasn’t worth the money I was paying.

text:
We gave Yelp every reason to work with us. A complete, polished profile. High-quality photos. Detailed service descriptions. Regular posts. Full case studies documenting our real work for real clients. We responded to every message. We even spent $1,000 on Yelp ads, because we wanted to do things properly.

Then, without warning, Yelp moved two legitimate 5-star reviews into their "Not Recommended" section—effectively hiding them from the public entirely.

These weren't throwaway reviews. They were detailed, genuine testimonials from verified customers. One reviewer posted video footage of the completed job. We built complete case studies around both projects. By any reasonable standard, these were exactly the kind of reviews a consumer platform should want to surface.

But here's where it gets difficult to accept: Yelp's official position is that they didn't remove anything. The reviews are technically still there. They're just hidden from everyone who visits your profile. That distinction—between "hidden" and "deleted"—may protect Yelp legally. In practice, the effect on your business is identical. Your credibility disappears overnight, with no warning and no explanation.

When we reached out to support, we were told it was "the algorithm." No escalation path. No appeals team. No resolution. Just a shrug wrapped in policy language.

Think about what that actually means for small business owners. You can invest months of effort, deliver outstanding work, earn genuine praise from real customers—and a platform's opaque automated system can silently erase that social proof while you're none the wiser. And when you ask why? There's no one there to answer.

Yelp frames this as consumer protection. But hiding authentic feedback from real customers doesn't protect consumers. It misleads them—while simultaneously punishing the businesses that earned those reviews fairly.

To any small business owner reading this: build your reputation on ground that won't shift beneath you. Your own website, your own testimonials, your own channels—places where your work speaks for itself without a third party deciding whether it deserves to be seen. If a platform profits from your ad spend while quietly undermining your credibility, the most rational response is to stop funding it. Redirect that budget somewhere your effort is actually rewarded.

If you absolutely need a third party resource, I'd go with a Google Business Profile and any number of social media platforms before ever considering Yelp.

My Experience With Yelp Advertising – A Warning for Small Business Owners

I am sharing my experience so other small business owners can make informed decisions before signing up for Yelp advertising services.

I was contacted by a Yelp representative and was assisted with setting up an advertising account. During this process, I provided payment information. However, I was never provided a contract by mail, never received a signed agreement, and, to the best of my knowledge, was never emailed any advertising agreement or terms and conditions.

Yelp offered promotional advertising credits as part of the account setup. During the advertising period, I began receiving messages that I believed were not resulting in legitimate business opportunities. In several instances, messages would be received, but after responding, there was no further communication. This raised concerns for me regarding the quality of the leads being generated.

Because of these concerns, I made the decision to cancel my Yelp advertising account. I have documentation showing that the account was canceled, and Yelp’s own records acknowledge the cancellation date.

Despite the cancellation, I was later charged $863. I disputed the charge and attempted to resolve the matter directly with Yelp. Unfortunately, I was unable to obtain a satisfactory resolution through customer service.

I subsequently filed a complaint with my state’s Attorney General’s office. Yelp responded to the Attorney General’s inquiry, but I remained dissatisfied with the company’s position and explanation regarding the charges.

Throughout this process, I repeatedly requested clarification regarding the basis for the charges and any agreement authorizing them. My concern remains that I was charged after cancellation despite my understanding that the account had already been terminated.

I encourage any small business owner considering Yelp advertising to:

• Carefully review all advertising terms and conditions.
• Request copies of any agreements in writing.
• Save all emails, account records, and cancellation confirmations.
• Monitor billing statements closely.
• Document all communications with representatives.
• Keep records of cancellation dates and account activity.

This post reflects my personal experience and opinions based on my records and interactions. Other business owners may have different experiences. I encourage everyone to conduct their own research and maintain thorough documentation when entering into any advertising agreement.

Business Owner,
TTR TAX & NOTARY CO LLC

• How the promotional credits were applied
• Detailed invoices and account ledger information
• Documentation supporting the final balance claimed

My recommendation to other business owners is simple: read every term carefully, monitor your account frequently, document every conversation, and obtain written confirmation regarding cancellation policies and promotional credits before spending any advertising dollars.

After this experience, I would not advertise with Yelp again and cannot recommend their advertising platform to other small business owners.

Better yet, don't do it.
